events.prelimNarrative: On October 22, 2026, about 1510 central daylight time, a Piper PA-28-160 airplane, N5393W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Claremore, Oklahoma. The flight instructor and student pilot were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 instructional flight. ADS-B data indicated that the flight departed from runway 18 at the Claremore Regional Airport (GCM) about 1431. The flight proceeded about 21 miles northeast of the airport at altitudes of up to about 3,500 feet mean sea level (msl). About 1455, the airplane reversed course and began to return to the airport. The final ADS-B data point was recorded at 1509:41 and was located about 2.08 miles east-southeast of GCM. The flight instructor reported that the student pilot leveled out at 2,500 feet to clear a tower about 5 miles east of the airport. After passing the tower, the student pilot continued the descent toward the airport traffic pattern. Shortly after reporting their position and intentions on the common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF), the engine lost power, although the propeller continued to windmill. Movement of the throttle control had no effect, and the flight instructor’s efforts to restore engine power were unsuccessful. At that point, the flight instructor set up for and executed a forced landing to a field about 2 miles east-southeast of the airport. Upon touching down on the field, he attempted to keep the nose wheel off the ground as long as possible. However, once the nose wheel touched down, it dug into the soft ground and collapsed. The airplane came to rest upright with damage to the fuselage, left wing, and nose landing gear. Airframe and engine examinations are planned once the airplane is recovered from the accident site.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 19, 2026, about 1703 central daylight time, a Consolidated Aeronautics Inc., Lake LA-4-200 airplane, N117RF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Springfield, Missouri. The pilot and pilot-rated passenger received minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that the airplane had been fueled about 30 minutes before he attempted to start the engine. He stated that when he engaged the engine starter, they heard and felt a large explosion from behind them. After several seconds, while shutting down the engine and airplane, they noticed dust and debris floating around them along with smoke. The pilot-rated-passenger also stated that their clothing was torn from the explosion. Video surveillance footage recorded shortly after the explosion showed light grey smoke emanating from the fuselage and both the pilot and pilot-rated-passenger were already outside of the airplane. The explosion and a subsequent interior fire resulted in substantial damage to the fuselage and empennage. Witnesses inside the nearby fixed base operator facility stated that the explosion rattled the building windows from about 300 ft away and was louder than a typical engine exhaust backfire. Postaccident examination of the fuselage hull revealed thermal damage to the interior structure of the lower right rear of the fuselage hull along with several burned electrical wiring bundles. Additional damage to the empennage hull and skin was observed with the skin being pillowed outward which was consistent with an overpressure event. The airplane was retained for further examination.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 18, 2026, about 1500 central daylight time, a Piper J3C-65 airplane, N88218, was involved in an accident near Boonville, Indiana. The pilot was not injured and a passenger in a vehicle that was struck by the airplane was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 personal flight. The pilot reported that he departed from runway 9 at the Boonville Airport (I91), and shortly afterward returned to make a low approach to runway 27. He flew in ground effect until reaching the west end of the runway where he climbed, performed an “impossible turn,” and glided toward runway 9. He then applied full throttle when he was on short final for runway 9 and entered a climbing right turn to establish the airplane on a left downwind for runway 27. He then made a descending 180° turn to final approach. The approach was steep and carried the airplane down the runway. The pilot flew in ground effect with minimal throttle until about 2/3 of the way down the runway where he applied full throttle. He kept the airplane in ground effect as airspeed increased. When at the departure end of runway 27 and still at a low altitude, the airplane impacted a car traveling northbound on South Baker Road, which passed along the west edge of the airport. The pilot stated that he did not see the car traveling northbound until it was in front of him due to tall weeds, shadows cast on the road by trees, and the dark color of the car. He attempted to pull up to avoid the collision but was not able to. The airplane continued to fly, and the pilot circled the airport for about 2 hours before landing on runway 9. The pilot estimated that the airplane’s speed was about 70 mph at the time of the impact. The pilot reported no preimpact mechanical anomalies that would have precluded normal operation. The left main landing gear was separated from the airplane during the impact. The right side of the car was impacted and damaged. The passenger of the car, who was seated in the front right seat was transported to the hospital with serious injuries and later succumbed to those injuries. The driver of the car and the pilot were not injured.

events.prelimNarrative: On October 17, 2026, about 1030 Pacific daylight time, a Maule M-7-260, N3217V, was substantially damaged during a runway excursion while landing at The Sea Ranch Airport (CA51), Sea Ranch, California. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. The pilot had recently retrieved the airplane from a maintenance facility following an annual inspection and associated maintenance. During the initial engine run-up, the right wheel brake remained engaged after he released the parking brake. He re-engaged the parking brake and released it again, after which both brakes released normally. He then taxied the airplane and completed the flight to CA51 without further reported brake anomalies. According to the pilot, after touchdown, the airplane pulled strongly to the right. The pilot applied the left brake in an attempt to counter the turn, but was unable to maintain directional control. The airplane departed the right side of the runway, traveled through a drainage swale, and struck an embankment. The airplane sustained substantial damage to both wings and the right-wing struts. The pilot reported that he believed the right parking brake may have re-engaged after he checked the brake pedals before landing. The airplane was retained for further examination.
